title: Should city centres be closed to cars?

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Did you see the council wants to close the whole central grid to private cars? Buses and deliveries only, from next spring.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: They've been threatening that for years. I'll believe it when the barriers go up.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: They did exactly this in Ghent, and the thing everyone forgets is that the shops fought it hard and then the footfall went up. Not down. Up.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Footfall going up doesn't mean the same shops survived, though. A butcher who loses his parking and gains a coffee crowd hasn't been helped.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It is, but you can phase it. Ghent took three years and moved the deliveries to early mornings. Nobody woke up to a wall.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: My worry is the ring road. If you squeeze the middle, all that traffic has to go somewhere, and where it goes is usually the cheapest housing.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: Mm, that's the bit I hadn't thought about.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: So the air gets cleaner exactly where the offices are, and worse where people actually live.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That can happen. It depends entirely on whether the public transport arrives before the ban does, and usually it doesn't.

turns.speaker: Tom
turns.text: Which is my whole objection, really. I'm not against it. I'm against doing it in that order.

turns.speaker: Aisha
turns.text: So none of us is against the idea. We just don't trust them to build the trams first.

points: The council proposes closing the central grid to private cars, leaving buses and deliveries, from next spring.
Daniel cites Ghent, where shopkeepers opposed the change and footfall then rose rather than fell.
Tom counters that higher footfall does not mean the same businesses survived, giving a butcher losing parking as an example.
Daniel argues for phasing it over years and shifting deliveries to early mornings, as Ghent did.

Tom's main objection is displacement: traffic squeezed out of the centre moves to the ring road and typically to cheaper housing, so air quality improves where offices are and worsens where people live.
They agree the idea is sound but object to the sequence, wanting public transport in place before any ban.
